content_voiceover: This slide is about the molecular basis you need for genotype questions: alpha thalassemia is caused overwhelmingly by deletions on chromosome sixteen, where there are normally two alpha-globin genes per chromosome, alpha-2 and alpha-1, giving four total per person. Alpha-thal-1, also called the alpha-zero form, deletes both alpha genes on one chromosome in cis, written as minus-minus over alpha-alpha; this is the dangerous genotype because if a carrier partners with another alpha-thal-1 carrier, offspring can inherit minus-minus on both chromosomes, which is hydrops fetalis. The Southeast Asian deletion, SEA, accounts for about ninety-five percent of alpha-thal-1 in Taiwan, with the Filipino and Thai deletions being rare alternatives. Alpha-thal-2, the alpha-plus form, deletes only one gene per chromosome in trans, written as minus-alpha over alpha-alpha, and is generally lower risk for severe compound disease. The most common alpha-plus deletion worldwide is minus-alpha-3.7, from a rightward crossover, followed by minus-alpha-4.2 from a leftward deletion. The board-relevant genetics point is cis versus trans: two single-gene deletions on the same chromosome, as in alpha-thal-1, is far more dangerous for producing HbH disease or hydrops in offspring than two deletions on opposite chromosomes, even though the total gene count lost is identical.
keypoints: Alpha-thal-1 (alpha0): both genes deleted in cis on one chromosome, minus-minus/alpha-alpha
SEA deletion = ~95% of alpha-thal-1 in Taiwan (vs Thai <1%, Filipino 4%)
Alpha-thal-2 (alpha+): one gene deleted in trans, minus-alpha/alpha-alpha
Cis deletions (alpha-thal-1) carry far higher reproductive risk than trans deletions
keypoint_voiceover: Remember the cis versus trans distinction. Alpha-thal-1, the alpha-zero form, deletes both alpha genes on the same chromosome, written minus-minus over alpha-alpha, and in Taiwan the Southeast Asian, or SEA, deletion accounts for about ninety-five percent of these cases. Alpha-thal-2, the alpha-plus form, deletes only one gene per chromosome, written minus-alpha over alpha-alpha, most commonly the minus-alpha-3.7 rightward deletion. The exam-critical point is that cis deletions, alpha-thal-1, carry a much higher risk of producing hemoglobin H disease or hydrops fetalis in offspring than trans deletions do, even though the same total number of genes is lost.
